words.definition: To imply an additional idea or feeling beyond a word's literal meaning.
words.example: For many people the word 'home' connotes warmth and safety, not just a building.
words.mnemonic: con- (with) + note — a word carries an extra 'note' along with it.

words.definition: To indicate or stand for something directly and literally.
words.example: On this map, a small red dot denotes a hospital.
words.mnemonic: de- (down) + note — it writes down exactly what is meant.

words.definition: The act of placing two things close together for contrasting effect.
words.example: The juxtaposition of the gleaming new tower and the crumbling church startled visitors.
words.mnemonic: juxta (Latin 'beside') + position — a position right beside something.

words.definition: Used in ordinary, informal conversation rather than formal writing or speech.
words.example: 'Gonna' is a colloquial way of saying 'going to.'
words.mnemonic: co-LOQUI-al — from 'loqui' (to speak); picture co-workers chatting casually.

words.definition: To introduce fresh methods, ideas, or products.
words.example: The startup hoped to innovate by replacing door keys with facial recognition.
words.mnemonic: in + nova (Latin 'new') — a nova is a bright new star; you bring in the new.

words.definition: Cleverly original and inventive in design or method.
words.example: She found an ingenious way to open the stuck jar using only a rubber band.
words.mnemonic: Hear 'genius' inside it — an ingenious solution shows genius.

words.definition: The quality of being clever, original, and inventive.
words.example: It took real ingenuity to build a working radio out of scrap parts.
words.mnemonic: in-GENIUS-ity — the state of having genius.

words.definition: New, original, and unlike anything known before.
words.example: The chef's novel pairing of chocolate and chili surprised the judges.
words.mnemonic: From Latin 'novus' (new); a story you've never read presents a novel idea.

words.definition: A person who is first to explore or develop a new area or method.
words.example: She was a pioneer of space medicine, studying effects no one had measured before.
words.mnemonic: Like the front-line foot soldier ('pion') who marches out ahead of everyone.

words.definition: To run a process using machines or software instead of people.
words.example: The factory decided to automate packing so workers could focus on quality checks.
words.mnemonic: auto (self) + mate — the machine takes on the task and does it by itself.

words.definition: An early sample or model built to test a concept before mass production.
words.example: Engineers crashed the car prototype repeatedly before approving the final design.
words.mnemonic: proto (first) + type — the very first type of a thing that gets made.

words.definition: To repeat a process, usually improving it a little each time.
words.example: The team iterated on the app, releasing a slightly better version every week.
words.mnemonic: From Latin 'iterum' (again); think of 'reiterate' — to say it again.

words.definition: To imitate someone admired in order to match or surpass them.
words.example: The young pianist practiced daily, hoping to emulate her idol's speed.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'imitate' with an E — a software emulator copies another machine.

words.definition: To make something larger or stronger by adding to it.
words.example: He took a second job to augment his monthly income.
words.mnemonic: From Latin 'augere' (to increase); 'augmented reality' adds to what you see.

words.definition: A point raised to oppose or challenge a previously stated position.
words.example: For every claim in the debate, she had a sharp counterargument ready.
words.mnemonic: counter (against) + argument — an argument that runs against yours.

words.definition: The quality of forming a unified, logical whole where parts connect clearly.
words.example: The essay's argument flowed so smoothly that its coherence impressed every reviewer.
words.mnemonic: Break it down: co- (together) + here — ideas that stick 'here together' hold together.

words.definition: To adjust something so it works as well as it possibly can.
words.example: Engineers reworked the code to optimize load times on slower phones.
words.mnemonic: From Latin 'optimus' (best) — you push something toward its 'opt'imum, its best.

words.definition: To convert physical records or signals into electronic form for a computer.
words.example: The library began to digitize its old manuscripts so anyone could read them online.
words.mnemonic: Turn it into digits (0s and 1s) — that's what the -ize ending does.

words.definition: To create a realistic imitation of a real process or situation, often for practice.
words.example: The flight software can simulate a storm so pilots train without real danger.
words.mnemonic: Hear 'similar' inside it — you make something similar to the real thing.

words.definition: To create or design something entirely new for the first time.
words.example: She hoped to invent a device that could purify water using only sunlight.
words.mnemonic: 'in + vent' — a fresh idea rushes in through the vent of imagination.

words.definition: A set of equipment or tools used for a particular purpose.
words.example: The chemistry lab's apparatus included beakers, burners, and tangled glass tubes.
words.mnemonic: Sound it out: 'a-pair-of-tubes' set up on the bench for an experiment.

words.definition: Designed to be practical and useful rather than attractive.
words.example: The office furniture was plain and utilitarian, built for work rather than show.
words.mnemonic: See 'utility' inside — it's all about utility, never about looks.

words.definition: To change in order to suit new conditions or situations.
words.example: Desert foxes adapt to scorching heat by hunting only after sunset.
words.mnemonic: 'add-apt': you add whatever is apt (suitable) for the new setting.

words.definition: To interrupt or throw into disorder a process or event.
words.example: Protesters tried to disrupt the meeting by shouting over the speakers.
words.mnemonic: 'dis + rupt' (rupture, break) — you break apart the normal flow.

words.definition: Causing disturbance or radical change to normal operations.
words.example: The startup's disruptive app forced older banks to rethink everything.
words.mnemonic: 'dis + rupt' (break) + -ive — a quality that shatters the status quo.

words.definition: Basic and undeveloped, involving only the simplest elements.
words.example: His rudimentary Spanish was enough to order food but not to hold a conversation.
words.mnemonic: 'rude-imentary' — a rude, rough, unfinished first draft of a skill.

words.definition: Highly developed, complex, or refined in design or thinking.
words.example: The camera used sophisticated software to sharpen photos taken in near darkness.
words.mnemonic: From Greek 'sophia' (wisdom) — such things carry deep, worldly cleverness.

words.definition: To state that something is true, often without offering proof.
words.example: The salesman would claim his pills cured everything, but doctors disagreed.
words.mnemonic: Hear 'exclaim' — you loudly announce that something is so.

words.definition: A person who supports and argues for an idea or cause.
words.example: As a leading proponent of solar power, she urged the city to ditch coal.
words.mnemonic: 'pro' (for) + 'ponent' (to put forth) — one who puts a case forward in favor.

words.definition: Strong, healthy, and able to withstand difficult conditions.
words.example: The bridge was robust enough to survive earthquakes and decades of heavy traffic.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'row-bust' — so tough it could bust through anything.

words.definition: Serving to test, prove, or provide evidence toward establishing whether something is true.
words.example: The detective set aside the gossip and focused only on the probative details: fingerprints, timestamps, and the muddy tire tracks.
words.mnemonic: Shares a root with 'probe' and 'prove' — a probative fact probes for the truth and helps prove the case.

words.definition: So strong or well-founded that it cannot be attacked, challenged, or disproven.
words.example: With three independent labs confirming the result, her conclusion stood unassailable against every critic in the room.
words.mnemonic: un + assail (to attack) + able — 'not able to be assailed,' like a fortress no army can storm.

words.definition: To raise trivial, petty objections or find fault over unimportant matters.
words.example: Instead of praising the ambitious plan, he chose to cavil about the font used on the cover page.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'gravel' — a caviler tosses tiny gravel-sized complaints into every conversation.

words.definition: The act of proving a statement or argument to be false or wrong.
words.example: The scientist's careful data amounted to a complete refutation of the rival theory, which soon vanished from textbooks.
words.mnemonic: Think 'refute' + '-ation' — the noun for the moment you shut down a claim with proof.

words.definition: Great skill or ability, especially in combat or a demanding activity.
words.example: The chess champion displayed such prowess that his opponents resigned within twenty moves.
words.mnemonic: Starts with 'pro' — a true pro shows off what they can do.

words.definition: Physical strength, energy, and healthy liveliness.
words.example: After a week of rest, she attacked the garden with such vigor that it was weeded by noon.
words.mnemonic: From Latin 'vigere,' to be lively — picture a tiger bursting out of its cage.

words.definition: To continue doing something firmly despite obstacles or discouragement.
words.example: Even after three rejections, he persisted and mailed his manuscript to a fourth publisher.
words.mnemonic: Break it: 'per' (through) + 'sist' (stand) — you keep standing through everything.

words.definition: To strongly desire something that belongs to someone else.
words.example: He coveted his neighbor's sports car, glancing at it enviously every single morning.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'cover it' — you want it so badly you'd hide it away under the covers.

words.definition: To dare to go somewhere or do something risky and uncertain.
words.example: They ventured deep into the cave, unsure whether the narrow passage led anywhere at all.
words.mnemonic: Hidden inside 'adventure' — a venture is the daring first step an adventure begins with.

words.definition: To focus attention obsessively on one single thing.
words.example: She fixated on the one negative review, ignoring the hundred glowing ones beside it.
words.mnemonic: Picture your eyes glued to a single spot, stuck fast and unable to look away.

words.definition: Widespread respect and admiration earned through achievement or quality.
words.example: Graduating from that university carries enormous prestige among the top employers.
words.mnemonic: Recall the magician film 'The Prestige' — the dazzling finale that leaves the crowd in awe.

words.definition: The state of being widely celebrated and honored by many people.
words.example: The violinist's renown spread until concert halls sold out on every continent.
words.mnemonic: Break it: 're' + 'known' — someone known again and again, everywhere.

words.definition: To move or climb upward to a higher position.
words.example: The balloon ascended until it was a tiny dot against the clouds.
words.mnemonic: 'A-scend' — think of an escalator carrying you steadily up.

words.definition: Incapable of producing any useful result; completely pointless.
words.example: Bailing the sinking rowboat with a teacup proved futile within a couple of minutes.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'few tiles' — roofing a whole house with a few tiles gets nowhere.

words.definition: Lacking skill; clumsy and awkward at doing things.
words.example: So inept with tools, he needed a full hour just to hang one picture frame.
words.mnemonic: 'In' (not) + 'ept' (as in 'apt') — not apt, therefore not able.
